lesson.title: K→CH Discrimination Drills
lesson.subtitle: Predict the ch-sound, derive unseen forms, and catch the k-impostors

hook.title: The Compass, Then the Impostors
hook.content: Two skills today. First, prediction: given any German ch-word, place its sound on the vowel compass — back vowel growls, front vowel whispers — before you ever hear it. Second, suspicion: not every German k is waiting to become a ch. Kirche (church), Rauch (smoke), acht (eight), Recht (right) already finished their journey — their ch hides English gh-words (kirk's cousin, reek, eight, right). And Latin loans like Kaffee and Kamera kept their hard k forever. The compass points at sounds; the impostor check points at history.

footnotes.title: The gh-Sisterhood
footnotes.content: acht/Recht/Nacht/Licht carry English eight/right/night/light — words where English spelled the gh and then stopped pronouncing it. German never stopped. When English speakers 'lost' the gh, they were only finishing a shift German had already made audible.

pattern.title: Derive, Then Verify
pattern.content: Derivation drill: make → machen (Ach), cook → kochen (Ach), break → brechen (Ich — front vowel e), book → Buch (Ach), milk → Milch (Ich via l). Impostor check: Kaffee, Kamera, Kind — hard k stays (Latin loans, or k in a safe position). And the finished-shift words: Kirche (church/kirk), Rauch (reek/smoke), acht (eight), recht (right) — their ch is the ghost of an English gh. One root, three costumes: k, ch, and silent gh.
pattern.linguist_note: The compass has one refinement: ch after consonants l and r takes the Ich-Laut even after back vowels (Milch, Kirche) — the consonant pulls the tongue forward with it.

exercises.prompt: Predict the sound: how does the 'ch' of 'brechen' sound?
options: Ach-Laut [x] — a throaty growl after a back vowel
Ich-Laut [ç] — a soft whisper after the front vowel e
exercises.target_answer: Ich-Laut [ç] — a soft whisper after the front vowel e
exercises.explanation: Front vowel e pulls the tongue forward: brechen, sprechen, Milch, riechen all whisper — and weich too, its k gone soft with the word for soft.

exercises.prompt: Match the ch-words with their English twins — the silent-gh set, plus two K → CH cousins. Then recall earlier vocabulary in the short phrases:

matching_pairs.german: Der Kuchen ist weich und süß
matching_pairs.english: The cake is soft and sweet

exercises.target_answer: acht, Recht, Rauch, Kirche, kauen, Knochen, Wir können riechen, Der Kuchen ist weich und süß
exercises.meaning: eight; right; reek / smoke; kirk / church; to chew; bone; We can smell; The cake is soft and sweet
exercises.explanation: English spelled the guttural gh and silenced it; German spells it ch and still sounds it. kauen is the mirror image: English chew shifted k to ch, German kept the k — the reverse of kirk/Kirche.

exercises.prompt: Which of these German k-words will NEVER become a ch — and why?
options: Kaffee — loanwords kept their hard k
exercises.target_answer: Kaffee — loanwords kept their hard k
exercises.explanation: The shift only hit native Germanic words standing in Germany around 500 AD. Kaffee arrived centuries later, k intact.

exercises.prompt: Derive unseen: English 'break' → German verb (mind the front vowel):
exercises.explanation: break → brechen: k → Ich-Laut [ç] after front vowel e (the vowel also widened to ei in the English twin).

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'The cook finds the cake sweet'
exercises.target_answer: Der Koch findet den Kuchen süß
exercises.meaning: The cook finds the cake sweet

vocab_hints.note: der Kuchen becomes den Kuchen as the thing found — the him-case arrives properly soon

exercises.explanation: The cook renders his verdict: der Koch findet den Kuchen süß — k softened to ch in his title, and süß keeps its ß from the sibilant shift.

summary.outcome: Predict Ach- vs Ich-Laut for any ch-word and identify k-impostors and finished gh-shifts.

use_example.german: Der Koch findet den Kuchen süß.
use_example.english: The cook finds the cake sweet.

summary.takeaway: The vowel steers the ch-sound; loanwords keep k; and Kirche, Rauch, acht, Recht are English gh-words still sounding their ghost.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the stop shift (D → T) — the consonant domino: day becomes Tag, drink becomes trinken.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from K→CH Discrimination Drills (The cook finds the cake sweet):
twist.target_answer: Der Koch findet den Kuchen süß
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Der Koch findet den Kuchen süß" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of K→CH Discrimination Drills without relying on short-term echo.

brechen.context_phrase: Ich will das Glas nicht brechen.
brechen.context_translation: I do not want to break the glass.
brechen.etymology_derivation: k → ch (Ich-Laut [ç] after front vowel e).

suchen.context_translation: I am looking for my glasses.
suchen.etymology_derivation: k → ch. Direct transitive object without prepositions.

buch.context_translation: I am reading a good book.

woche.context_phrase: Nächste Woche fahre ich nach Berlin.
woche.context_translation: Next week I travel to Berlin.

kirche.etymology_derivation: Greek kyriakon → Scottish kirk / German Kirche.

rauch.context_phrase: Wo Rauch ist, ist auch Feuer.
rauch.context_translation: Where there is smoke, there is also fire.

kauen.context_phrase: Kau dein Essen langsam und gut.
kauen.context_translation: Chew your food slowly and well.
kauen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *keuwan, PIE *ǵyewh₁-; the page lists English chew as cognate — English palatalized the old k to ch, German kept it as k. [wiktionary]

knochen.context_phrase: Der Hund kaut an einem Knochen.
knochen.context_translation: The dog is chewing on a bone.
knochen.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *knokō 'bone, joint' — cognate with English knuckle; German k shifted to ch. [wiktionary]

riechen.etymology_derivation: From Old High German riohhan, from Proto-Germanic *reukaną. English reek is a listed cognate, keeping the k where German shifted to ch. [wiktionary]

koch.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *kok — a true k → ch shift word (cook ↔ Koch). [wiktionary]

süß.context_phrase: Der Kuchen ist zu süß für mich.
süß.context_translation: The cake is too sweet for me.
süß.etymology_derivation: süß — from Proto-Germanic *swōtuz, PIE *swéh₂dus, exactly cognate with English sweet; the final t shifted to ß and the old w was lost before the rounded vowel. [wiktionary]

solch.etymology_derivation: k → ch (Old English swylc ↔ German solch).

bleich.context_phrase: Er wurde vor Schreck ganz bleich.
bleich.context_translation: He turned completely pale with fright.

handwerker.etymology_derivation: Hand (hand) + Werker (worker); Werk comes from Proto-Germanic *werką (PIE *wérǵom) - the exact ch-twin of English work. [wiktionary][etymonline]

stockwerk.context_phrase: Die Küche ist im ersten Stockwerk.
stockwerk.context_translation: The kitchen is on the first floor.
stockwerk.etymology_derivation: Stock (stick, then storey) + Werk; Stock is the twin of stock and Werk the twin of work (k to ch) — a storey is literally a stock of the house. [wiktionary]

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: Explains make ↔ machen, cook ↔ kochen, break ↔ brechen, book ↔ Buch, and week ↔ Woche.
k_to_ch.literature_source: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.
